turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): alright ruth, come on through. sorry about the wait, he's stuck on that computer again.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): oh that's fine, we were out there forever and I was telling denise they moved the handicap spots, so I had to walk, which, um, with these feet was not ideal.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I drove her. I come weekday mornings, I don't live with her.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): let me get a blood pressure before he comes in. arm out. try not to talk for a sec.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): mm. I brought the home cuff numbers, they're in the blue notebook, not the black one, the black one is coupons.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): okay. blood pressure is 164 over 96. pulse is 78.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): that can't be right. at the kitchen table this morning it was 130 over 82, I wrote it down.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I watched her. it was 132 over 80. she ran it twice.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): hey, sorry, one second, this screen just froze. uh. okay. what brings you in?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): well, where do I even start, the left shoe, I bought those back in march, and now I can't even...
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): sorry, say that again? I clicked the wrong chart. what's the main thing?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): my ankles are all swollen, and I'm running to the bathroom all day.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): swollen ankles. how long?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): about three weeks. I've had high blood pressure for years, that's not why I came, but the ankles started as a little sock ring in the evenings and now it's both of them all day, the left one more, and my shoes leave a dent.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): it got worse after they changed her blood pressure pill. I keep telling her that.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): right, the high blood pressure. which pill. hold on, the list is loading.
[SEG0017] person_1 (NURSE): on the med list I have amlodipine five milligrams once a day, and hydrochlorothiazide.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): no, that's the old dose. they bumped the amlodipene to ten. the bottle says ten milligrams, one every morning with my coffee.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): can you repeat that dose? the cursor jumped.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): ten milligrams. one tablet every morning. I set the pill box up on mondays. the water pill is twenty-five.

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): yes, hydrochlorthiazide, twenty-five milligrams, also in the morning, and then I pee and pee. sometimes eight or nine times before lunch, and I get up twice at night, even if I skip my tea.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): any pain or burning when you pee?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): no burning, no pain. just often. the stream seems fine, I mean I'm not measuring it or anything.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): any fever?
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): tell him about the shoes not zipping, you were going on about that in the car.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): oh. no fever. I checked yesterday with that thermometer from the drugstore, it said 98.4.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): lungs wise, any cough, wheezing, shortness of breath?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): no, none of that. there was a little tickle last month from the neighbor's cat but that was nothing, no cough now.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): what about your weight, any change?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): umm I don't know. the scale sticks, sometimes it says I'm up a couple pounds, sometimes it doesn't, I really couldn't tell you.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): yeah, don't trust that scale. it jumped six pounds in one day. nonsense.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): mm. right. let me see the ankles. shoes off.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): the left is the stubborn one. I sleep with a pillow under my feet and in the morning it's a little better, then by dinner it's back, which is annoying when we have...
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): both ankles are puffy. it pits when I press. pulses in the feet are fine.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): see, I knew it wasn't just thick socks. I ordered those beige compression things and they roll down and leave a worse groove, so I quit wearing them.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): I think the swelling is from the amlodipine. that medicine does this pretty often.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): but then what about my pressure, the home numbers are decent and yours aren't, and if you stop it won't I just...
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): we're going to stop the amlodipine. I'll start losartan, fifty milligrams, once a day, in its place.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): what about the water pill? she can't be sprinting to the bathroom at the senior center, they have one stall.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): keep the hydrochlorothiazide, twenty-five milligrams, every morning. same as now. don't move it to nighttime.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): so the water one stays with breakfast. and losartan, is that the one that starts with an l, because my sister takes something and she never stops talking about it...
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): yes. losartan fifty milligrams once a day. I'm also ordering a basic metabolic panel today, kidneys and electrolytes.
[SEG0043] person_1 (NURSE): I can draw that before you leave. lab's still open.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): good. put your feet up in the afternoon. if you get dizzy, or the swelling suddenly gets a lot worse, call us.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): and the peeing, is that just my life now? eight times in a morning, I timed it, I was late to my hair appointment last tuesday and she gave my slot away.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): the water pill is doing that. morning is the right time. we'll see you back in two weeks and look again.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): two weeks. should I bring the notebook? I write the date, the top number, the bottom number, sometimes a little star if I felt funny.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): bring the notebook, yes. sorry, what was that home reading again? I never typed it.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): 132 over 80. this morning.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I had 130 over 82 in my head, but she was watching, so she's probably right.
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): okay. we'll use today's clinic pressure for the chart. reception will book the two weeks.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): thank you. I'll try not to talk the poor girl's ear off during the blood draw, last time I got going about my tomatoes and the tube...

spec.situation: Patient on amlodipine and a water tablet with swollen ankles and passing urine often; blood pressure read at clinic and at home with different numbers; doctor changes one medicine.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Caregiver says she comes weekday mornings and doesn't live with her; not described as a home aide.
bad.text: living (description=A home aide comes weekday mornings and does not live with her, status=current, reported_by=caregiver)

bad.reason: Doctor says amlodipine will be stopped, so not currently used after plan.
Dose discrepancy is discussed, but transcript does not state it remains unresolved.
bad.text: The nurse reads amlodipine as 5 mg once daily while the patient says the dose is 10 mg once daily. (type=medication_discrepancy, related_entities=medications[0], resolution_status=unresolved)

omissions.text: Amlodipine current dose is 10 mg, one tablet every morning; the recorded medication entry for amlodipine is missing the dose and the old 5 mg list entry was corrected by patient/caregiver.
Patient denied pain with urination as well as burning ('no burning, no pain').
Home blood pressure readings reported this morning were about 130/82 per patient and 132/80 per caregiver after two checks.
Swelling progression/detail: started as a little sock ring in the evenings and progressed to being present in both ankles all day; shoes leave a dent.
Compression stockings were tried but rolled down and left a worse groove, so she stopped wearing them.
Urinary frequency persisted even if she skips tea.
Temperature was checked at home yesterday and was 98.4.
The nurse planned to draw the ordered basic metabolic panel before the patient left because the lab was still open.
Doctor explained that the urinary frequency is due to the hydrochlorothiazide ('the water pill is doing that').
